lead: Greens powders are powdered blends of vegetables, algae, herbs, vitamins and minerals mixed into water as a daily supplement. The best-known brand is AG1, formerly Athletic Greens, a Nevada-based company founded in December 2010 by Chris Ashenden that sells a roughly 75-ingredient powder by subscription.[1] People take it as an all-in-one daily nutrition step, with the idea that better micronutrient intake shows up as healthier-looking skin, hair and nails, and as energy for training.

Healthline's review describes AG1 as containing 75 vitamins, minerals, probiotics and plant compounds in four proprietary blends, with a serving of 12 g providing about 50 calories and high amounts of some vitamins such as B12 and biotin.[2] Its reviewer, who used it daily for about a month, reported her nails seemed to grow faster, noted no other changes, and said blood work would be needed to see measurable effects.[2]

AG1 is marketed heavily through podcasts and influencers, with creators paid through affiliate arrangements.[1] Critics quoted in coverage, including a Harvard Medical School professor, have described the supporting trials as very small, and have questioned the value of a many-ingredient blend.[1]

chain: Daily mixed vitamin, mineral and plant powder
Broader micronutrient intake (including biotin and vitamins)
Users report healthier-looking skin, hair and nails and more energy to train
angle.text: People take a greens powder as a one-scoop daily routine for general nutrition, hoping it supports skin, hair and nail appearance and recovery. Reports of such effects are mainly personal accounts.

infobox: About US$79 per month on subscription, US$99 one-time pouch[1][2]

paras: Healthline reports AG1 includes spirulina, adaptogens such as ashwagandha and rhodiola, mushroom powders and two probiotic strains, in proprietary blends whose exact amounts are not disclosed. It contains no vitamin D or iron.[2] Per serving it lists B12 at 917 percent and biotin at 1,100 percent of the daily value.[2]

The company began with one product sold directly to consumers by subscription; its formula was changed more than 50 times between 2010 and 2024. It rebranded as AG1 in December 2021 after hiring Kat Cole as president and COO. Reported revenue rose from about US$160 million in 2021 to about US$600 million in 2024, and the company was valued at US$1.2 billion in January 2025.[1]
Ashenden resigned in 2024 after earlier criminal convictions in New Zealand became public, and Cole became CEO.[1]

Podcasters including Tim Ferriss were early promoters, and Ferriss later became an investor.[1] JoAnn Manson of Harvard Medical School called the company's supporting trials very small, dietitian Charlotte Martin argues that so many ingredients make the amount of any single nutrient small, and Jonathan Jarry of McGill University says the blend has little scientific backing relative to its cost. Critics also note that some ingredient amounts are hidden within proprietary blends.[1] Healthline says the product lacks research confirming safety or effectiveness, while some individual ingredients have research that is often limited or does not apply to the strains or doses used.[2]

Some users report upset stomach, bloating and diarrhea, possibly from probiotics or inulin, and Healthline advises caution for people who are pregnant, breastfeeding, taking certain medications or have medical conditions.[2]
No studies found examining greens powders for appearance outcomes. Commentators describe the company's own supporting trials as small.[1][2]

timeline.event: Athletic Greens founded by Chris Ashenden.[1]
Rebrands as AG1; Kat Cole joins as president and COO.[1]

name: Greens powders (AG1)

card.summary: A heavily podcast-marketed daily greens drink whose supporting trials are small and whose appearance effects are untested.
card.note: Some ingredient amounts sit inside proprietary blends; cost is about US$79 per month (2024).

quick.overview:
Greens powders are mixed-ingredient powders (vegetables, algae, vitamins, minerals) taken as a daily drink. AG1 is the leading brand and is sold by subscription, mostly via influencer and podcast promotion.

Critics quoted in coverage call its supporting trials very small. No studies were found on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The product supplies a broad mix of micronutrients and plant ingredients; claimed benefits are general-health ones, and critics argue each ingredient is present in small amounts.
quick.risks: No specific harms are described in the sources used here. Reported issues are cost and proprietary-blend labelling that withholds some ingredient amounts.
